summary: Learners come to see a ratio as a MULTIPLICATIVE relationship — one quantity is always a constant number of times the other — and to recognise this same relationship in three forms: a ratio a:b, a fraction a/b (x is a/b of y), and a linear function y=kx whose constant multiple k is the gradient and whose graph is a straight line through the origin. For the worked ratio 1:3 (x:y), x is 1/3 of y and y=3x, where the gradient 3 is y÷x. The central work is distinguishing a multiplicative relationship (constant ratio/multiple) from an additive one (constant difference). Vary the quantities, surface what stays the same (the multiple), and read the invariant across ratio tables, double number lines, graphs and a perceptible context such as paint shade. Keep part-to-part ratio a:b (x is 1/3 OF y) distinct from part-to-whole fraction (x out of the total x+y).
misconceptions: Reads a relationship additively — fixes on the difference between a pair of values ('y is 4 more than x') instead of the constant multiple
Sees the constant multiplier for whole-number rows but cannot express it as a ratio, fraction, or y = kx
Confuses the part-to-part ratio a:b with the fraction a/b of the whole
Thinks any straight-line graph shows proportionality, not noticing it must pass through the origin

activities.title: One ratio, three costumes — and what breaks under 'add 4'
steps: Work with the ratio 1:3 (e.g. red:yellow paint) and extend a ratio table: 1:3, 2:6, 3:9, 4:12, scaling both quantities together.
For each new row, plot the point (x,y) on a coordinate graph and note that the points fall on a straight line passing through the origin (0,0).
Observe a perceptible constant-ratio context alongside: in an idealised, thoroughly mixed model, a paint swatch mixed in that ratio keeps the same orange shade as the batch grows.
Name the same relationship in three forms on this one example: ratio 1:3, fraction/multiple (y is 3 times x; x is 1/3 of y), and linear function y=3x with gradient 3 (the gradient equals y÷x).

Switch the rule from multiplicative (y=3x) to additive (y=x+4) and watch what changes: the graph's line no longer passes through the origin, the plotted points leave the straight proportional line, and the swatch shade shifts row by row.
State in your own words which quantity stays constant in each case — the MULTIPLE stays fixed for a ratio relationship, while the DIFFERENCE stays fixed for an additive one.
activities.insight: A ratio is a single multiplicative idea wearing three costumes (ratio a:b, fraction a/b, straight line y=kx through the origin); its signature is a constant multiple, not a constant difference. When the quantities scale, the difference changes but the multiple — and the colour, the ratio and the gradient — stay the same. An additive rule breaks the line-through-origin and changes the shade, which is what separates it from a ratio.

activities.title: Read the ratio table both ways
steps: Take a ratio table and read DOWN the columns to find the scalar multiplier (how each row scales from the previous).
Read ACROSS the rows to find the constant functional relationship a:b / the y=kx rule between the two quantities.
Use a double number line aligned at 0 so that equal ratios line up, and check that both lines start at aligned zeros.
Given x=10 for a 1:3 relationship, work out y directly using the multiplier (×3) rather than extending the table row by row.

Distinguish 'x is 1/3 OF y' (part-to-part, the correct multiplicative reading) from 'x is a fraction of the whole x+y' (part-to-whole); for example, with 2 red : 5 blue beads, red is 2/5 of the blue count (part-to-part) but 2 out of 7 total beads (part-to-whole), anchoring each reading to its own picture.
activities.insight: A ratio table encodes both a scalar multiplier (down columns) and a functional multiplier (across, the y=kx rule); the multiple can be used directly to predict any value. A double number line aligned at zero shows equal ratios lining up. Part-to-part and part-to-whole are different comparisons.

activities.title: Sort and match: is it a ratio relationship?
steps: Sort several tables of values into 'ratio relationship' vs 'not a ratio relationship', justifying each by whether y÷x is constant.
Match equivalent forms: connect 1:3 with y=3x and with a straight line through the origin.
Predict y for a new x in a given table, with an additive answer offered as a tempting but wrong option, and explain why the additive choice fails.
Given two graphs, identify which shows proportionality and explain that it must pass through the origin.
Test a tricky table — x=2,y=5 and x=4,y=7 — and decide whether it is a ratio relationship (it is additive: +3 each time, but 5÷2 ≠ 7÷4, so no constant multiple).
activities.insight: Sorting and matching across forms, with deliberate additive distractors, can check whether a learner can translate among ratio, fraction and linear form and can reject an additive table as not proportional. A straight-line graph only shows proportionality when it passes through the origin.

activities.title: Justify it: times or more than?
steps: Face a mentor who presents tables and asks for each: 'is it times, or more than? How do you know?'
Defend your classification by pointing to the constant multiple and showing that the difference changes down the table.
Respond to a scaled counter-case when you give an additive answer — e.g. 'you said +4; check the next row, does +4 still work?'
Explain, before mixing any paint, whether a 2:6 batch will be darker, lighter or the same shade as a 1:3 batch, and why.
activities.insight: Being pressed to justify whether a relationship is multiplicative or additive, and to meet a scaled counter-case, brings the reasoning into the open and can check whether the learner gives the right answer for the right reason.

checkQuestion: Here is a table of matching values. When x = 2, y = 6; when x = 3, y = 9; when x = 5, y = 15. I want two things. First: is y always the same AMOUNT bigger than x, or always the same number of TIMES x? Second, and most important: how can you tell from the table which one it is?
checkAnswer: y is always the same number of TIMES x — y is 3 times x (y = 3x). You can tell because the AMOUNT bigger changes (6 is 4 more than 2, 9 is 6 more, 15 is 10 more) so it is not a constant 'more than', but y ÷ x is always 3, a constant multiple — this is the multiplicative relationship, the ratio x:y = 1:3.
